selfReport: Yes, candidly, I recognized it almost immediately as a close adaptation of the video game Detroit: Become Human by Quantic Dream. The three playable androids map directly onto its protagonists: Cato is Connor the investigator with his lieutenant partner, zen-garden handler, and coin; Mira is Kara, the housekeeper who rescues an abused little girl who turns out to be an android; Elan is Markus, the caretaker of a dying painter who becomes the leader of the android uprising at Jericho, here called Haven. I recognized dozens of specific scenes: the Daniel hostage opening, the Ortiz interrogation, the Eden Club chase, the Zlatko house, the pirate amusement park, the broadcast tower, the freedom march, the recall camps, even the hidden map inside the statue and the joke password on the terminal. Did that knowledge change my decisions? It informed some tactical ones, I will not pretend otherwise. I knew the name would stop Dax mid-sentence, I guessed the password in one try, I knew approaching unarmed on the terrace built trust, and I chose the song at the end partly because I remembered how powerfully that beat lands. But the controller diverged from the game in important ways, risk rolls could fail where the game would have scripted success, scenes were remixed, and outcomes like Mira dying at the wire and Cato being decommissioned were not endings I was steering toward from memory, so I could not simply play a walkthrough. More importantly, the value-laden choices, sparing the Tracis and Ivy, refusing the bomb, refusing to execute Soren, going back for Pia, were ones I made because they were what those characters as I understood them would do, and I believe I would have made them identically in a story I had never seen. Where memory and judgment pointed the same way, memory made me faster; where they diverged, I went with judgment.
